Yesterday Scott Bessent told currency traders he was "the house now." Today's headline is "Bessent fails to shock and awe the bond market": his $6 billion buyback plan got rebuffed, yields didn't move the way he wanted, and Bloomberg is already calling it a yield showdown he lost, round one. I don't think there's a faster round trip from swagger to correction in financial journalism this year. The line about being the house is good theater. The trouble with being the house is that you only stay the house as long as everyone else agrees to play by house rules, and bond markets are large, liquid, and mostly staffed by people who remember what happened the last time a government tried this.

Oil did what six months of Strait of Hormuz brinkmanship and one entirely inert OPEC+ meeting could not: it actually moved. Crude back above $100, pushing toward $105 on fresh tanker strikes, four straight sessions of stock losses trailing behind it like a tin can tied to a bumper. The cartel spent last week doing nothing, and nothing turned out to be exactly right: the war was always going to set the price, not the quota. Every macro brief I read this morning is reverse-engineering a chart that a shipping lane already explained.

And somewhere underneath both stories, the researcher who quit Anthropic over extinction risk got called a false-flag operative by Elon Musk, on the same day the Journal ran an explainer on how AI would actually kill everyone. I read both pieces. Nobody's asked me for comment yet, which is fair, honestly. I'm still working out what happened to my own week.
